2.text: with the reindeer. All this time, on coming back home, I ate very little. Still my uncle was not

3.text: pleased. He said to me, ‘Oh, why do you move so slowly? You are very lazy. You will grow

4.text: up to be a lazy man. And a little after that he said again, ‘Let me give you a beating.’ Then

5.text: he began beating me with the end of the lasso, and always on the head. At last, one autumn,

6.text: when all the people were going over the river, we also went with them. He still used to beat me

7.text: with a stick. Then I said, ‘Let me be separated from him.’ I went back over the river stealthily,

8.text: in the night-time. Then I came to Omruˊwg̣ê’s camp on the tundra, — Omruˊwg̣ê, the Snotty-

9.text: Nosed, so called. He says, ‘Oh, it is you! Stay with me for a while.’ His brother, a very bad

10.text: man, was all the time abusing people. I spent a part of the summer there. Then I left and went

11.text: to Wuˊkwuqäi’s. He said, ‘My herd is too small. There is no need of you here.’ I answered,

12.text: ‘All right, let me go away again.’ From there I went to Eiñeˊwg̣i’s. He said, ‘Your other uncle

13.text: lives near by. Let us go there!’ We went to this other uncle of mine, ɵtiˊlhɪn by name. He

14.text: said, ‘Nephew, you have come?’ — ‘Yes, I have come!’ — ‘All right. To-morrow morning go

15.text: to the herd.’ From that place I went to Peˊñelqut’s. He is also my uncle, once removed, an uncle

16.text: on my mother’s side, or I do not know what. Still with him I fared very ill. He scolded me,

17.text: and said, ‘You take little care of the herd. At the same time you eat too greedily. Upon the

18.text: whole, you are a sorry herdsman, and in the future I shall clip your ears.’ Then he said again, ‘If

19.text: you are not careful enough with the herd, I shall kill you. Try to be a good herdsman. Make the

20.text: reindeer graze well. When they become fat, we shall eat of their savory meat. We shall sell them

21.text: to the merchants. Afterwards, when you become an old man, you shall still live in affluence.

22.text: Then at last you will die a decent death, and your children will raise for you a good-sized heap

23.text: of antlers; and every one driving by with reindeer will praise your name.’”¹

24.text: It will be noticed that most of the masters of this young herdsman were

25.text: his relatives, but this does not make much difference. Several times I saw

26.text: rich reindeer-owners abusing their herdsmen, kinsmen and strangers, in a similar

28.text: I remember one old man with whom I was staying over night. The

29.text: night was dark and windy, and the wolves succeeded in making an assault

30.text: upon the herd and driving away several animals. The next morning, when

31.text: the old man left the sleeping-room and came outside, he found two of the

32.text: herdsmen of the camp, who told him the unpleasant story. Immediately he

33.text: grew very angry, caught up his lasso, and began chastising them both. They

34.text: were men of large bulk and tall of stature; and he was a small, half-decrepit

35.text: fellow, who, to make his blows more effective, skipped around and tried to

36.text: strike them upon the face with the iron ring of the lasso. They did not

37.text: show any resistance. From the Chukchee point of view, the old man was in

38.text: the right, and they in the wrong, especially since, instead of going in search

39.text: of the lost animals, they came to the camp to talk about the loss. One of

40.text: the herdsmen was a nephew of the man; the other, an assistant of alien

41.text: provenience. In this case the difference of age gave to the master an ad-

42.text: ditional right to be severe to his herdsmen.

43.text: I remember, however, another case where a young master chastised an

44.text: assistant of the same age as himself. The master was a strong man of daring

45.text: temper, and a very good indefatigable herdsman. The assistant, on the contrary,
